subtype: Approach: presenting an unexpected result honestly [Revision]
passage: Sit, beta. Your grandmother Reena has a story about a bean plant. When I was ten, we grew beans for the school fair. I put one pot in the dark cupboard and wrote on my paper that it would stay green. It grew, but pale as chalk. My classmate Ganga whispered, "Change it, write green." I nearly did. Then I thought, the plant did not lie, so why should I? At the fair I stood by my board and said, "I guessed green, and it turned pale, and that surprised me." The old teacher judging asked why. I said I did not know yet. He gave me a ribbon, but I remember his smile more.

qa.q: What colour was the plant that grew in the cupboard?
What was Reena feeling when Ganga whispered to change the paper?
qa.a: She felt tempted and uneasy, since she nearly did it and then reasoned that the plant had not lied.

qa.q: What choice did young Reena make at the fair, and why did it work out?
qa.a: She chose to show the pale plant and say she was surprised, and the judge valued her honesty enough to give her a ribbon.

qa.q: How did the judging teacher see Reena's answer that she did not know yet?
qa.a: The teacher seems to have taken it as honest work, giving her a ribbon and a smile.

grounding: A child keeps her unexpected pale-plant result and explains her surprise instead of changing the results.

subtype: Approach: presenting an unexpected result honestly [Revision]
passage: The morning of the science fair, the bus broke down, and Lalremsiami arrived twenty minutes late with her two bean plants wobbling in a box. Her prediction had been that the cupboard plant would not grow at all. It had grown, long and thin, but it was pale yellow. On the bus she had thought about hiding it and showing only the window plant. Or saying it was green in real life. But when Santosh sir, the judge, stopped at her table, she put both plants in front of him. "I thought this one wouldn't grow. It did. But it's pale. That surprised me. I want to find out why." Santosh sir leaned closer. "That's the most interesting thing I've heard today."

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami arrive twenty minutes late?
How did Lalremsiami feel on the bus about the pale plant?
qa.a: She felt tempted and anxious, thinking about hiding it or changing the story, before choosing to be honest.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami do next with the surprising result?
qa.a: She could read or ask why plants in the dark turn pale, and plan a new test to check the reason.

qa.q: How does the honest result look to Santosh sir?
qa.a: Santosh sir is interested and impressed, calling it the most interesting thing he has heard that day.

grounding: It shows a girl presenting a pale plant that did not match her prediction honestly and explaining what surprised her instead of changing the result.

subtype: Approach: presenting an unexpected result honestly [Revision]
passage: Alka's poster for the science fair said, in big letters, "Plants need light to grow." But her cupboard plant had grown, tall and spindly and pale. The night before, in their flat in Kochi, her cousin Jomon looked at it and said, "Just cut it short. Nobody will know." Alka looked at the plant for a long time. "That's not what happened," she said. She took a marker and added a question mark to her poster title. Under it she wrote: "It grew, but it was pale. Why?" At the fair a teacher asked why her result was different from her prediction. Alka pointed at the pale leaves and explained exactly what surprised her. She didn't win, but the teacher asked her to join the science club.

qa.q: What did Alka add to her poster title?
How did Alka feel when Jomon suggested cutting the plant short?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and torn for a moment, then firm that she would show what really happened.

qa.q: What else could Alka try to understand her result?
qa.a: She could repeat the test and measure both plants' colour and height every day, so she can see when the difference appears.

qa.q: How does Alka's choice look to the teacher at the fair?
qa.a: The teacher values her honesty and curiosity, enough to invite her to the science club.

grounding: It shows a child deciding to present an unexpected pale plant as it was and explain what surprised her rather than change the result.
